items.Semantic name: Crustal buoyancy and load-support context
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Derive the mechanical support and buoyancy available to the lithosphere from retained crustal structure, density, strength, and accumulated loads. This is the supporting state for deformation, not an independent geological event.
items.Observable effects: Supported cratons, thickened mountain roots, overloaded forelands and sediment-laden basins respond differently when tectonic or surface loads act; these contrasts ultimately become stable uplands, flexural basins and broad arches.
items.Fields & products read: Retained continental/oceanic crust composition and thickness; crust age and mechanical properties; material density; overlying sediment, water and ice loads; inherited structural state and present load context.
items.Fields & products written: Derived support/buoyancy target or effective stiffness context for flexure, relaxation and uplift. It owns no newly formed rock, mountain, tectonic event or historical deformation.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Read-only lithosphere/material provider exposed through typed support/load questions; changes in Ground, water, sediment, ice and crust invalidate this context for consuming processes.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: At each applicable mechanical evaluation on World or a finer map, based on that map's captured/current physical state. No elapsed-time evolution by itself.
items.Other process interactions: Consumed by lithospheric flexure, crustal relaxation and uplift; receives physical state from orogeny, volcanic loading, erosion/deposition, grounded ice and marine loading.
items.Invariants / obligations: Derive from actual inherited/current materials and loads; never inject unexplained height or duplicate deformation. Re-evaluating unchanged state is idempotent; historical causation belongs to consuming processes.
items.Review notes: Non-process derived-state contract: define the whole mechanically meaningful support context, not the current support-target function as a standalone geological process.

items.Semantic name: Post-orogenic crustal relaxation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Relax accumulated tectonic deformation and crustal roots over genuine geological time, allowing previously thickened or loaded crust to spread, subside, rise or adjust in response to material strength and surrounding support.
items.Observable effects: Young steep ranges give way to wider, lower highlands; foreland basins or uplifted margins persist and evolve; old orogenic belts retain recognizable but altered root and relief signatures.
items.Fields & products read: Retained rock columns, root reserves and deformation history; tectonic activity and elapsed geological duration; material rheology/strength; inherited elevations, topographic load and lithospheric support.
items.Fields & products written: Adjusted crustal/root distributions and effective relief/load state, with material movement or deformation booked through the Ground owner; retained relaxation history where it matters.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Uses the lithospheric support and rock-material response vocabulary, not a separate arbitrary elevation smoothing pass. Mechanical relaxation modifies later support/flexure and erosion forcing.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Time-dependent World geological evolution after construction/loading, active where deformation and material response warrant it. On children, resolve finer inherited relaxation geometry without re-aging the crust.
items.Other process interactions: Responds to orogenic construction, tectonic uplift, flexure and sediment/ice load; exposes changing slopes and basins to erosion, climate and drainage.
items.Invariants / obligations: Relaxation must follow actual stressed material and available deformation; do not erase geological ancestry, conserved source identity or named peaks. A child must not relive its parent's millions of years of relaxation.
items.Review notes: Separate semantic phenomenon from active mountain construction: stored crustal deformation continues changing relief after compressive forcing weakens.

items.Semantic name: Load-driven lithospheric flexure
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Bend and rebound the mechanically supported lithosphere under spatially distributed rock, sediment, volcanic, ice and water loading and unloading.
items.Observable effects: Foreland troughs develop beside mountain belts, forebulges and broad coastal arches arise around loads, ice-loading depressions can recover, and ancient basins influence drainage and later sediment accumulation.
items.Fields & products read: Crustal support/rigidity and root structure; spatial loads from rock mountains, sediments, volcanic deposits, grounded ice and water; inherited bedrock geometry and boundary load context.
items.Fields & products written: Flexural deflection and supported bedrock/elevation state, plus deformation history when genuine loading changes over geological time; no creation of rock merely from bending.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Consumes the derived crustal-support contract and material/load providers. Its response feeds back into depositional accommodation, coastal position, runoff and future loading.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World historical episodes with load changes and appropriate mechanical scale; at child refinement, resolve the present flexural geometry from inherited support and external loads without running old loading history again.
items.Other process interactions: Orogeny and volcanism add load; sedimentation, water and ice redistribute load; relaxation and uplift change stiffness; drainage and ocean basins respond to deflection.
items.Invariants / obligations: Deflection must be spatially connected to real loads/support and respect the retained crust and material owner. Do not invent independent subsidence waves or force numerical identity with the coarse parent elevation.
items.Review notes: Distinguish bending under loads from tectonic uplift, crustal spreading and erosional removal.

items.Semantic name: Connected-ocean inundation and sea-stand realization
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Determine which water is connected to the ocean and establish sea surfaces, depths, water bodies, and marine continuity.
items.Observable effects: Connected marine basins flood to a physically grounded sea stand while isolated depressions remain lakes. Changing relief, grounded ice or sea level opens and closes straits, drowns lowlands, exposes shelves and shifts the coast, creating consequential changes to ocean access and habitat.
items.Fields & products read: Retained ground/bedrock elevation and basin topology; the world's existing marine-water budget and sea-level datum; grounded ice and ice-water storage; sea-stand forcing; previous marine/lake stores and remembered reconnections; captured boundary ocean connectivity and source conditions.
items.Fields & products written: Effective marine sea stand, ocean versus enclosed-water occupancy, water depths and surface elevations, connected water-body identities and marine/lake continuity state. The state can change as land or ice changes; its own operation does not erode or deposit rock.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Shared sea-stand and water-column ownership couple crustal deformation, ice, water budget and inundation. Outside-footprint ocean connection is an explicit boundary input; ocean state supplies the coastline seen by currents, waves, atmosphere, drainage and ecology.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World formation sets the initial ocean-water budget; subsequent world stages resolve the sea on changed physical geography. Region, coastal City and Street maps realize the inherited present sea stand and offshore connections at finer scale, without establishing a new independent global ocean or advancing a historical era.
items.Other process interactions: Tectonic basin construction, shelf change, glacial sequestration/melting and sea-level forcing alter connected marine extent; connected water governs coasts, shelf ecology, estuaries, ocean heat, maritime travel and downstream sediment reception.
items.Invariants / obligations: Marine water must be connected to a legitimate sea boundary/source; disconnected inland depressions do not become oceans by crop artifact. Respect the already established water budget and outside-ocean context, retain relevant named seas/coasts and avoid reliving marine history when resolving a finer present map.
items.Review notes: Composite hydrologic state-realization responsibility: initial water budget, effective sea stand, connected inundation and marine/lake continuity belong together. This is not four independent causal processes and does not itself cause geomorphic erosion.

items.Semantic name: Gravity-driven slope failure and downslope material redistribution
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Move unstable rock and loose sediment downslope under gravity, reshaping hillslopes according to material and terrain resistance.
items.Observable effects: Fresh scarps, slumps, landslides, talus, colluvial aprons and gentler unstable hillslopes appear where uplift, incision, glacial retreat, saturation or other disturbances oversteepen material. Exposed beds and deposited debris alter later erosion and habitat.
items.Fields & products read: Actual elevation and slope; retained rock and loose-sediment columns, cohesion and weathering; fractures and undercut faces; water saturation, frost and ice; stabilizing roots and vegetation; inherited slope-failure history and material present at the footprint edge.
items.Fields & products written: Material-aware downslope transfers and deposits; revised ground surface/bedrock exposure and sediment thickness; failure scars, debris accumulations and available downstream sediment supply, with source provenance and later slope susceptibility retained.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Ground/material operations determine which intact or loose layers can move; root-hold, wetness and slope-stability questions connect ecology, hydrology and rock mechanics. Transport follows real topography and respects the same material ledgers as rivers and ice.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: A geomorphic mechanism during genuine World historical change and when Region/City/Street refinement exposes finer unstable slopes. A present-state relaxation uses inherited material and new geometry, not an invented additional epoch of slope history; demands outside-footprint deposition context where needed.
items.Other process interactions: Uplift, tectonic fracturing, river incision, shore undercutting, glaciation/retreat and earthquakes trigger instability; sediment transport and subsequent soil/vegetation succession receive the released material and exposed substrate. The same phenomenon may be invoked at several schedule positions.
items.Invariants / obligations: Never move rock as anonymous height or replace it with cosmetic noise. Source material, destination, receiving space and altered stratigraphy remain real; rooted slopes resist appropriately, talus does not become intact bedrock, and repeated execution on unchanged stable slopes creates no further erosion.
items.Review notes: Canonical physical phenomenon. One mass-wasting contract covers pre- and post-incision slope readjustment; different occurrences or resolution strategies do not create a second semantic process.

items.Semantic name: Present continental-margin and offshore sediment frame
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Characterize the sea-facing margin, its tectonic origin and its offshore reach on the current coast, so marine sediment and shoreline processes receive spatially correct context; actual shelf and slope evolution belongs to physical processes.
items.Observable effects: A continental margin's geological character remains legible at its current shore and across its neighboring seabed. Passive, convergent, rifted or transform coasts have distinct offshore settings and sediment destinations, without inventing new relief merely by classifying them.
items.Fields & products read: Present marine connectivity, shore position, elevations and submerged depth; persistent tectonic margin identity and crustal ancestry; external shelf/basin context beyond a selected footprint; relevant named geographic entities.
items.Fields & products written: Derived present-shore margin character, offshore distance and coastal-margin context/provenance for downstream coastal and marine deposition processes. Does not independently add rock, remove bedrock or alter the ocean budget.
items.Shared questions / coupling: A derived coastal-margin frame mediates between tectonic origin/current physical geography and wave abrasion, shelf transport, marine settling and coastal-place characterization. Structural margin classification is not synonymous with current wet/dry shoreline.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Current-state interpretation on World and finer maps wherever marine shore or shelf context matters. Reads external marine geography when a Region/City/Street footprint clips the shelf; no historical elapsed-time behavior or extra epoch of margin construction.
items.Other process interactions: Tectonic uplift, subsidence, rifting and volcanic coasts establish structural margin history; sea-level changes expose another piece of it. Marine deposition, coastal erosion, currents, Pressure-related coastal effects and geographic publication consume the resulting present margin frame.
items.Invariants / obligations: Do not rewrite tectonic ancestry when a coastline migrates, treat an artificial child-map edge as the continental shelf break, or mutate rock to calculate a margin category. The frame must describe the actual source-connected coast and remain consistent with inherited major marine geography.
items.Review notes: This entry is best treated as derived present-day context, despite its historical 'evolution' name. Actual geomorphic margin evolution is produced by tectonics, load response, marine sedimentation and coastal erosion; do not add a parallel unmotivated reshaping process.

items.Semantic name: Seabed sediment transport, settling and stratigraphic accumulation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Accumulate and deposit marine sediment on submerged ground, particularly along continental shelves and margins.
items.Observable effects: Shallow-shelf muds and sands, depositional wedges, basin fills, sediment drapes and buried former seabeds develop from the marine supply and bathymetry. Sediment accumulates in sheltered or low-energy zones and may travel farther down submarine slopes.
items.Fields & products read: Marine cargo actually supplied by rivers, coasts, ice and prior seabed erosion; bathymetry, shelf gradients, connected marine water, currents/wave exposure, relative sea level, carrier capacity and existing sedimentary strata. Where the modeled sea is cropped, incoming suspended load is an explicit boundary condition.
items.Fields & products written: Seabed deposits and retained material packages with source composition, sediment thickness and accumulated stratigraphic history; any remaining suspended or moving marine load is routed onward or retained in the specified boundary reservoir. Seabed elevation and future burial conditions respond to these deposits.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Receives sediment through the physical material/cargo contract; wave/current and depth questions determine mobility and accommodation space. River sediment exchange and coastal processes supply and redistribute the same material rather than spawning independent seabed matter.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World historical marine phases when there is actual load and deposition time; at Region/City/Street, spatially resolve inherited shelf and seabed strata and condition local marine morphology on supplied cargo without reconstructing past epochs. Influence extends along connected marine paths and across map edges.
items.Other process interactions: River mouths, deltas, coastal erosion, ocean circulation, glacial outwash and submarine gravity flow provide or relocate sediment. Burial/lithification later converts suitable deposits; shoaling and shore evolution respond to changed seabed geometry.
items.Invariants / obligations: Seabed deposits must be physically supported by cargo, water coverage, transport paths and accommodation space; retain provenance, grain/material distinctions and the difference between deposition, resuspension and burial. No arbitrary seafloor blanket or duplicate deposition at every refinement.
items.Review notes: Distinct marine material-transport/deposition phenomenon, not an ocean-presentation routine; link river-to-sea material handoff and external marine supply to the same retained cargo ownership.

items.Semantic name: Faulting and connected crustal fractures
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Create, reactivate and propagate tectonically driven faults and rock fractures through structurally suitable materials, retaining permeability and damaged zones as consequences of strain.
items.Observable effects: Connected fault systems, rift faults, fractured ridge belts, geothermal conduits, displaced rock and spring/groundwater corridors provide recognizable landscape structure and causal paths for later processes.
items.Fields & products read: Plate/margin deformation and orientation, accumulated tectonic strain, existing faults and inherited weakness, rock strength/fabric, thermal and overburden context, spatially extended fault endpoints.
items.Fields & products written: Retained fault/fracture traces, damaged or weakened material and fracture conductance/permeability, plus appropriate structural influence on terrain and flow; named features only where significant.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Fracture connectivity couples tectonics and the retained Ground material to groundwater, geothermal transport, volcanic vents and Fire's mineral-core conduits. Other domains consume conductance, not a magic-specific fault subclass.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World geological deformation, formation and reactivation with real forcing; children elaborate finer fault branches conditioned by existing structural state and external continuation without recreating past earthquakes.
items.Other process interactions: Tectonic margins, sutures and uplift provide stress; volcanism and geothermal flows use apertures; weathering, erosion, aquifers and magical Fire use resulting connected pathways.
items.Invariants / obligations: Faults must be supported by stress, strength or inherited weakness and form plausible connected structures. Preserve established faults and geology; no arbitrary noise scratches, duplicate fractures or unsupported long-distance transport.
items.Review notes: One causal fracture/fault phenomenon; permeability and trace interpretation are consequences, not unrelated processes.

items.Semantic name: Geothermal heat and hydrothermal circulation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Express internally generated and retained terrestrial heat through the crust, especially where tectonic activity, plume sources, intrusive rocks and connected fractures allow upward transport and water-mediated release.
items.Observable effects: Hot spots, warm springs, geothermal corridors, thawed valleys and altered rock have plausible positions and gradients; thermal landscapes can persist after eruption, shaping settlement, erosion, ice and magical Fire origins.
items.Fields & products read: Plume-root strength, volcanic/intrusive thermal state, crust age and thermal history, rock conductivity, fractures, groundwater/water pathways and impact residual heat; inherited geothermal conditions.
items.Fields & products written: Geothermal heat/heat-source intensity and hydrothermal influence made available to physical climate, ice and fluid receivers, with persistent geological heat/alteration where causally produced.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Heat and groundwater/rock transport connect to shared thermal questions. Magical Fire may use geothermal conduits and store heat in cores, but geothermal physics and Fire's material stocks remain separate owners.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World historical source/heat evolution when energy is produced or released; current-state interpretation on Region/City/Street where existing deep sources and pathways support local vents and warmth.
items.Other process interactions: Fed by tectonic and plume activity, volcanism, impacts and fracture connectivity; influences atmospheric warmth, hydrothermal water, glacial melting, alteration and Fire source eligibility.
items.Invariants / obligations: No active local heat without a supported source or transport path; avoid treating magical Fire as a generic replacement for ordinary geothermal heat. Finer maps may resolve vents without minting new historical heat reservoirs.
items.Review notes: Semantic heat-transport/expressivity contract: the geothermal potential query is only one implementation strategy, not the definition of this phenomenon.

items.Semantic name: Continental collision and suturing
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Join and deform distinct continental crustal ancestries where they collide, leaving persistent sutures, seams, thickened and altered crust and mechanical contacts that later mountain building can reactivate.
items.Observable effects: Old collision belts, contrasting rock terranes, deep structural seams, inherited mountain spines and persistent zones of weakness or strength reveal continental assembly even after plates have moved on.
items.Fields & products read: Plate convergence and contact geometry, distinct continental assembly/material ancestry, strain, thickness, rock properties, pre-existing seams and geological duration.
items.Fields & products written: Retained crustal suture identities, contact strength/continuity, collision intensity and deformation of the involved retained materials, with provenance tied to the meeting crustal ancestries.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Ground material owner retains actual suture/terrane history; tectonic contact and lithosphere questions expose strength to mountain-building, flexure and fracture processes.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World-scale geological collisions over epochs; subsequent child maps resolve local structural grain from inherited sutures without re-colliding the source continents.
items.Other process interactions: Plate motion initiates collision; orogeny, uplift and fracture propagation respond to suture geometry; erosion and metamorphism expose seams; later tectonics may reactivate them.
items.Invariants / obligations: A historical suture must remember **which continental materials joined**, distinct from whichever present-day plate carries them. No free-standing decorative suture line without a collision or inherited seam.
items.Review notes: Keep continental ancestry, present plate membership and enduring suture contact as separate concepts.

items.Semantic name: Evolving tectonic margin regimes
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Determine and evolve the physical character of active and abandoned tectonic margins—collision, subduction, spreading, rifting, transform motion and passive margins—from plate relations, crust history and deformation.
items.Observable effects: Active margins develop coherent arc/trench/rift belts and strain zones, while older passive or abandoned contacts leave shelves, subsiding edges, eroded scarps and age-structured crust.
items.Fields & products read: Relative plate motion and contact geometry, crust type/thickness and age, tectonic strain and history, oceanic maturity, continental ancestry, inherited boundaries.
items.Fields & products written: Current margin regime/geometry, crust-age and activity context, and mechanistically supported subduction/rift/transform forcing for downstream material processes; physical effects remain owned by the processes performing them.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Margin classification is a derived view of evolving tectonic contacts; causally significant regime/age changes are part of this tectonic phenomenon. Expose typed forcing to orogeny, volcanism, fractures and continental shelves.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World geological epochs as contacts open, close, migrate or cease; finer maps resolve present regime and existing history without moving entire plates anew.
items.Other process interactions: Plate genesis and motion set margin dynamics; sutures mark older collisions; uplift, volcanism, fracture networks, coastal erosion and marine basins respond to regime changes.
items.Invariants / obligations: Do not equate a visible coastline with a plate boundary, nor today's plate with continental ancestry. A passive margin cannot acquire active-subduction effects solely because it is near a shore.
items.Review notes: Boundary regimes must be grounded in actual plate contacts; interpretation of the margin and history of changing contacts are one architectural responsibility.

items.Semantic name: Continental structural-domain context
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Derive broad continental interior, boundary and crustal-affinity context from retained tectonic ancestry, crustal architecture and current deformation so other processes can distinguish where their mechanisms are applicable.
items.Observable effects: Stable cratonic interiors, inherited continental belts and mechanically active margins have different development potential; their broad organization influences relief and erosion rather than creating a second labeled landmass.
items.Fields & products read: Crust composition/thickness, tectonic provinces and continental assembly identities, inherited rock structure, strain, boundary regime and retained geologic history.
items.Fields & products written: Derived continental potential/domain descriptors supplied to tectonic uplift, mountain construction and material response; no new rock, plates, material stocks or autonomous geological event.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Read-only structural context provider. Continental potential is not the same as land/sea classification; queries are invalidated by genuine tectonic or crustal changes.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Computed as needed for World geological processes and finer current-state conditioning from each map's inherited/current crust. No independent elapsed-time step.
items.Other process interactions: Used by tectonic uplift, orogenic construction, flexure, fracture susceptibility and significant landscape interpretation. State originates in province genesis, collision, material history and erosion.
items.Invariants / obligations: Domain context must follow real crustal ancestry and deformation, not random continental-label masks. No mutation or double-booked tectonic history as a side effect of asking for this provider.
items.Review notes: Non-process structural context contract within the tectonics family; don't create a standalone world-forming process just because it has a query identity.

items.Semantic name: Tectonic uplift and broad crustal thickening
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Elevate, tilt and thicken continental and oceanic crust in response to genuine tectonic forcing, buoyancy and regional structural constraints, creating broad-scale topographic change before narrower mountain-belt construction.
items.Observable effects: Rising plateaus, uplifted coastal benches, high continental shoulders, rift-flank relief and renewed old highlands reshape watersheds, climate exposure and the physical setting of later mountain ranges.
items.Fields & products read: Active plate/margin forces and strain, continental-domain context, retained crustal thickness/materials, lithospheric support, pre-existing relief, deformation history and geological time.
items.Fields & products written: Rock-column/thickness changes, supported bedrock uplift or subsidence, associated deformation/load and long-lived broad relief; derived surface heights follow retained physical state.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Consumes tectonic and support questions; works through the Ground/crust owner rather than writing arbitrary visual height. Flexure and erosion must observe the changed structural substrate.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: During real World tectonic episodes; child Region/City/Street work may expose finer inherited uplift structure but may not invoke fresh continental plate-motion history.
items.Other process interactions: Plate collisions, rifting and flexure supply forcing; orogeny builds localized peaks over the broad rise; drainage, climate, glaciers and erosion respond to new relief.
items.Invariants / obligations: Physical uplift must be supported by crustal structure and force, with material/load consequences; it is not a noise-based mountain overlay. Retain inherited plate/root history and named major relief without exact parent-height fitting.
items.Review notes: Separate broad tectonic uplift from focused orogenic mountain construction, though their mechanisms and material response can cooperate.

items.Semantic name: Genesis of tectonic plates and continental ancestry
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Establish the initial tectonic provinces, crustal affinities, continental assemblies and oceanic domains that supply a coherent structural starting state for the world's later plate motion and material history.
items.Observable effects: Continents, ocean basins, stable cores, distinct accreted terranes and plausible plate-scale boundary geometry acquire a causal tectonic organization before mountains, arcs and marginal basins develop.
items.Fields & products read: World seed and geography controls, initial land/crust budget and physical scaling, admissible province geometry and boundary constraints; no completed world-history snapshots to replay.
items.Fields & products written: Stable IDs for plate/province structure and continental assembly ancestry, initial continental/oceanic crust distribution, plate geometry and potential motion, material/rock initialization inputs.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Initial province/assembly state feeds tectonic-motion, margin, suture and crust genesis mechanisms; this is world formation, not arbitrary runtime workspace initialization.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World genesis before subsequent geological epochs. Finer maps inherit the final structural ancestry and resolve its existing local consequences; no independent plate genesis on every child.
items.Other process interactions: Material genesis follows structural allocation; motion, subduction, suturing, orogeny, volcanism, rifting and basin history accumulate from this starting condition.
items.Invariants / obligations: Maintain distinct continental ancestry and current plate ownership; seed one coherent tectonic world rather than unrelated plate labels. Child refinement cannot invent new global assemblies or discard established tectonic identities.
items.Review notes: Semantic world-forming genesis process even if scheduled once. Do not classify it as generic startup plumbing.

items.Semantic name: Mountain-belt construction and ridge development
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Build mountain belts and individual high-relief structures from convergent tectonics, crustal shortening, material stacking, inherited structural grain and localized reactivation.
items.Observable effects: Coherent mountain chains show varying relief, distinct ridges and prominent summits rising above their ridge averages, thrust fronts, hanging valleys, passes and neighboring foreland basins instead of uniform raised ribbons.
items.Fields & products read: Compressional strain, convergence/sutures, tectonic provinces, crustal roots and material budget, rock strength/fabric, orogenic history, inherited structural relief and elapsed geological forcing.
items.Fields & products written: Placed/thickened or displaced rock in retained Ground, crustal root reserves, mountain uplift/ridge influence, deformation history and named-relief support where significance warrants it.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Material modes/ledger handle construction from existing or formed crust; lithospheric support, flexure and relaxation react to accumulated loads; ridge/peak morphology derives from structure, not a post-hoc naming mask.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World geological mountain-building intervals; finer maps reveal local peaks, folds, cliffs and passes from inherited belt/root structure at their physical resolution, not an additional full orogenic epoch.
items.Other process interactions: Plate convergence/suturing create forcing; volcanism can add ridgeline rock; flexure and relaxation shape load response; glacial/fluvial erosion cuts the constructed rock and reveals differentiated peaks.
items.Invariants / obligations: Do not substitute a uniform uplift field for actual mountain construction. Peaks can exceed the ridge's mean supported relief. Preserve inherited major mountain identities while allowing physical local elaboration.
items.Review notes: One orogenic process may compose crustal shortening, root building and ridge-shape strategies; avoid retaining each helper as an unrelated process.

items.Semantic name: Volcanic eruptions and igneous landscape construction
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Create and modify terrain through magma supply, eruption, intrusion, lava emplacement, ash/debris deposition and caldera formation at appropriate tectonic or persistent mantle-plume sources.
items.Observable effects: Distinct volcanoes, island arcs, cones, calderas, lava fields, volcanic plateaus, altered ground and ash-fed slopes affect drainage, coastlines, ecosystems and places. Dormant or eroded volcanoes retain identifiable rock history.
items.Fields & products read: Subduction and spreading/transform context, mantle plume roots, magma/thermal supply, fracture pathways, current surface/rock material, water/ice and explicit geological episode.
items.Fields & products written: Actual igneous material/rock columns and surface lava/ejecta, volcanic edifices and collapse basins, heat and stress history, source consumption or renewal and qualifying named volcanic features.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Rock emplacement and fracture/heat effects pass through shared physical material operations; volcanism supplies ordinary geothermal heat and may create eligible conduits for Fire, but it does not generically manufacture Fire magic stock.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: At appropriate source-supported World geological intervals; child maps realize inherited lava paths and local cone/caldera structure without repeating the parent eruption.
items.Other process interactions: Receives plume and margin dynamics, crustal fracture paths and lithosphere context; feeds flexure/loading, coasts, soil fertility, climate, ice, water, ecology and Fire-source opportunities.
items.Invariants / obligations: No volcano without a plausible magma source and route. Deposits and relief must be causally linked and retained as geological material; no repeated eruption merely because a child map is generated.
items.Review notes: Preserve the distinction between magma-generated rock and the magic Fire medium; they may interact through fractures and heat, but are not interchangeable.

items.Semantic name: Impact excavation, ejecta and shock geology
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Model discrete impact events as physically localized excavation and redistribution of target material, creating rims, breccia/ejecta aprons, shocks and lasting structural and thermal aftermath.
items.Observable effects: Crater basins with raised rims and discontinuous ejecta, impact lakes, damaged rocks and radial fractures stand out from ordinary volcanic calderas and may seed fallen Fire-core deposits when that system is enabled.
items.Fields & products read: Actual impact event position, size and episode; existing rock stratigraphy/resistance, relief, water/ice cover, local structural context and inherited impact history.
items.Fields & products written: Excavated/redistributed material and shock-altered strata, crater/rim geometry, impact heat/fracture history, retained impact event identity and qualifying named crater or ring features.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Rock/material excavation and deposition use the Ground owner; fracture and heat consequences feed geology, climate, erosion, basins and optional magical Fire's **fallen-core origin**.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Discrete World historical impact events of declared physical scale, with local affected footprint and time-specific residuals; finer maps resolve retained impact morphology without striking the same spot again.
items.Other process interactions: Cratering interacts with erosion, glaciation, groundwater, volcanic-like landforms and lithospheric loads; impact-derived Fire cores remain distinct from fracture-fed geothermal cores.
items.Invariants / obligations: A given event excavates only once in history. No duplicate craters from repeated refinement; preserve actual relocated material, recognizable impact causation and named significance.
items.Review notes: Separate impact event occurrence from subsequent slow erosion of its ring, burial of ejecta and later magical/thermal effects.

items.Semantic name: Genesis of retained rock and crustal materials
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Create the first materially coherent rock substrate and crustal columns from the world's nascent tectonic architecture and source material budget, giving later processes actual rocks to deform, move, weather and expose.
items.Observable effects: Old shields, younger margins, oceanic crust and varied lithologic provinces differ in mechanical strength, erosion resistance and mineral character; later cliff, ridge and basin forms arise from this material foundation.
items.Fields & products read: Tectonic province/assembly structure, initial crust and oceanic/continental allocation, rock-material definitions, volcanic/intrusive source context, formation seed and physical unit scale.
items.Fields & products written: Initial retained rock columns/material shares, crustal structure, competence/fabric and parent support or load conditions; base stratigraphy/history sufficient for later material transport and metamorphism.
items.Shared questions / coupling: One-time world/material genesis supplies the shared Ground owner; all subsequent tectonic, volcanic, erosion, metamorphic and transport operations use these same retained materials rather than a second synthetic terrain substrate.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World formation before tectonic and landscape evolution. On a refined map, its counterpart is **rock-state inheritance and local material realization**, not deleting the parent's strata and reinitializing a pristine world.
items.Other process interactions: Plate/province genesis conditions rock types; collision, uplift, faults, volcanism and weathering transform them; downstream ecology, rivers, soil and magic read actual substrate.
items.Invariants / obligations: Do not reset inherited Ground, crust histories, existing material reservoirs or established geography on refinement. Every newly represented rock package needs an origin and physically meaningful context.
items.Review notes: World-forming semantic process, not a generic workspace initializer; child material realization belongs to inheritance/state realization rather than re-running this genesis.

items.Semantic name: Persistent mantle-plume source formation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Form spatially persistent deep thermal/melt sources that can repeatedly influence crustal magmatism and local heat as surface plates migrate across them.
items.Observable effects: Hotspot chains, off-boundary volcanic islands, broad igneous provinces, geothermal provinces and old extinct cones reveal the relationship between durable mantle sources and moving overlying crust.
items.Fields & products read: World tectonic/province context, admissible deep-source geography, initial mantle supply parameters, source placement/history and moving crustal pathways.
items.Fields & products written: Retained mantle-plume root locations/strengths and lineage plus ongoing heat/melt-supply potential and source-associated geological history; volcanic edifices are written by downstream volcanism.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Plume source is independent of present plate label; eruption/heat mechanisms consume its supply through shared physical source contracts. Fracture and crust permeability govern expression at the surface.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World genesis and real geological continuation across tectonic epochs; finer maps inherit existing plume sources and resolve affected rock/heat without seeding an unrelated local root.
items.Other process interactions: Moving plates over roots drive volcanic construction and hotspot tracks; geothermal flow changes ice/water and can enable Fire veins; flexure/erosion expose historical volcanic chains.
items.Invariants / obligations: Persistent deep sources must not be regenerated on each child or drift with every surface feature. Differentiate mantle source identity from its many episodic crustal volcanic expressions.
items.Review notes: An initial source-founding behavior is a legitimate part of a semantic mantle-plume process.

items.Semantic name: Scale-conditioned shoreline morphology realization
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Resolve the inherited coastline and its causal margin history into finer supported relief, bays, headlands, shoals and shoreline irregularity as detail becomes geographically expressible.
items.Observable effects: Broad coastlines develop recognizable coves, embayments, offshore rocks, small headlands, coastal escarpments, shelves and natural landing opportunities at finer scales; features follow geological and erosional character rather than being arbitrary shoreline jitter.
items.Fields & products read: Captured coast and sea stand; retained nearshore elevation and rock columns, strength, fractures and tectonic margin; ocean-wave/current exposure and historical erosion/deposition; named shoreline landmarks and external context within a meaningful coastal halo.
items.Fields & products written: Finer spatial realization of coastal elevation, seabed/bedrock exposure, supported shoreline shape and associated derived geomorphic context. Newly resolved minor coastal features remain local to the child; inherited named coasts and coastal landmarks retain identity.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Tectonic margin, wave climate, sediment distribution and rock structure jointly constrain local morphology. Shoreline detail changes the physical surface that coastal erosion, ocean connection, water routing, habitats and settlement access subsequently read.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Present-state refinement / small-feature realization at World-to-Region-to-City/Street resolutions where the coast can support additional detail. It is not another pass through elapsed geological history; a coast-free interior map has no shoreline work.
items.Other process interactions: Continental margins and uplift set coast character; abrasion, marine deposition, deltas, storms and Pressure create localized shoreline structures; wetlands, ports, fisheries and coastal settlements respond to the resolved terrain.
items.Invariants / obligations: Do not invent unrelated random coastal patterns, displace established named coastal landmarks out of their physical setting or replay historical erosion on each child. Resolve coastal detail from inherited material and prior causes; any true rock transport belongs to a material-aware process.
items.Review notes: Refinement/state realization, not an independent epoch of erosion. The semantic contract is causal coastline detail conditioned by retained geography; broad noise-only perturbation is not an intended standalone geological phenomenon.

items.Semantic name: Plate-motion and deformation activity
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Advance the changing tectonic force field through genuine geological epochs as plates move, contact, converge, slide, subduct, split or separate, with strain and boundary regimes responding to actual geometry and material resistance.
items.Observable effects: Mountain fronts migrate or quiet, rifts open, crustal contacts weld or tear, volcanic arcs relocate, and geologically active belts differ from old inert boundaries; retained deformation history helps explain current landforms.
items.Fields & products read: Current plate/province positions and motions, continental ancestry, contact strength, crust/rock resistance, existing fractures and sutures, inherited tectonic history and geological elapsed time.
items.Fields & products written: Updated tectonic position/contact/activity, boundary type and direction, compressive/extensional/shear strain, tectonic forcing for rock/heat processes and retained activity history.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Supplies the shared causal tectonic forcing to margin evolution, sutures, uplift, orogeny, fractures and volcanism. It does not silently advance those processes or reset support history whenever a query is read.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: During World geological epochs when time is explicitly advanced, across plate-scale neighborhoods and physical contact boundaries. Regional/city/street refinement uses pinned completed tectonic history and present strain context only.
items.Other process interactions: Province genesis initializes movers; contacts and crustal properties feed back into motion; uplift, fracture, volcanoes and sutures consume strain; erosion and material transport change later mechanical resistance.
items.Invariants / obligations: Only real geologic-time events advance plates and strain. Keep continent ancestry distinct from moving plate membership; never restart continental motion for a child's local detail pass.
items.Review notes: Semantic responsibility is dynamic tectonic forcing, not merely an 'epoch' scheduling wrapper. Keep history/forcing distinct from registry activation.

items.Semantic name: Land-ice accumulation, ablation and glacier extent
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Accumulate or melt land ice from local temperature, precipitation, and terrain, retaining ice thickness and balance.
items.Observable effects: Snow accumulation builds ice caps, mountain glaciers and valley tongues where climate and relief allow; sustained warmth or heat produces retreating margins, bare glacial forelands and proglacial water. Long-lived ice leaves a recognizable glacial footprint even after retreat.
items.Fields & products read: Temperature and seasonal snowfall/moisture, precipitation supply, elevation and land relief, inherited ice thickness/extent and persistence, geothermal or magical heat/retention, marine/freshwater boundaries, elapsed climate interval and upstream ice context.
items.Fields & products written: Retained IceThickness and IceBalance, retreat/ablation and maximum historical ice extent/thickness, land/freshwater ice storage and its released-water obligation; downstream ice-flow and geographic interpretation inputs.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Atmospheric snow/cold and geothermal warmth set ordinary balance; Aurora persistence and Fire heating affect the applicable ice/thermal rules through shared physical questions. Exchange melt and stored-water changes with hydrology and sea-level budgets rather than materializing water independently.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Historical World glacial intervals advance true accumulation or loss over elapsed time. Finer Region/City/Street maps condition current ice extent and local boundaries on captured parent history and external catchment/ice supply; additional terrain detail is not permission to repeat centuries of ice growth.
items.Other process interactions: Ice flow redistributes accumulated mass; glaciers abrade bedrock and carry till; meltwater feeds runoff, lakes and sediment transport; the changing ice load and melt volume affect coasts, groundwater, ecology, navigation and settlements.
items.Invariants / obligations: Ice mass must have snowfall, imported ice or inherited stores as an origin, and ablation must have an explicit fate. Preserve enduring ice masses across cropped child maps; distinguish present extent from historic maximum and never replay a completed ice age during refinement.
items.Review notes: Semantic owner of ice accumulation and ablation, not of flow routing or rock cutting. Keep land/freshwater glaciation distinct from marine sea-ice formation, while allowing typed thermal and material interaction.

items.Semantic name: Glacier motion, ice flux and grounding
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Route the movement of land ice across terrain, establishing flow directions, flux, and grounded ice conditions.
items.Observable effects: Flowing ice tongues occupy valleys and troughs, converge from tributary glaciers, thicken where movement slows and leave fast-flow corridors or stagnant ice; persistent flow directions help explain subsequent scoured valleys and moraine locations.
items.Fields & products read: Retained glacier thickness and ice-surface elevation, basal terrain and slope, ice temperature/rheology and basal resistance, grounded/floating conditions, climate-driven accumulation, elapsed time, boundary ice inflow and inherited flow history.
items.Fields & products written: Ice transport flux and directions (IceFlux, IceFlowTargets), grounded-ice state, maximum/historical flow records, and transported ice/thickness where explicit elapsed dynamics require redistribution; boundary mass-flux outputs.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Transport consumes ice supplied by mass balance and exchanges actual ice mass across the domain. Grounding and basal traction determine erosion potential; cold/persistence and heat influence mobility via shared material/physical responses, not magic-specific copies of flow code.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World glacial development over geological/climatic episodes, with regional flow fields resolved where the map supports more detail. A refined crop receives cross-boundary glacier supply and downstream outlet conditions and does not restart a completed glacial motion history.
items.Other process interactions: Mass balance establishes stored ice; motion determines abrasion/plucking intensity, subglacial drainage, debris paths, terminus position and glacial sediment deposition; lake and ocean interfaces govern calving and grounding.
items.Invariants / obligations: Transport redistributes rather than creates ice. Grounded, floating and stagnant ice have distinct effects; a glacier entering a cropped region cannot disappear because its headwaters lie outside the footprint. Retain physically coherent inflow/outflow and historical maximum flow.
items.Review notes: Keep the kinematics and mass transport in one semantic process even when coarse or fine strategies differ. Glacial erosion is a separate material-changing response to grounded moving ice.

items.Semantic name: Glacial abrasion, plucking and bedrock excavation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Remove and entrain exposed rock and sediment through moving ice and its contact with the land.
items.Observable effects: U-shaped glacial valleys, broad troughs, hanging tributaries, cirques, overdeepened basins, scoured bedrock and fjord-ready valleys remain visible long after the glacier has retreated. Different rock strengths create asymmetric carved relief.
items.Fields & products read: Grounded ice location, thickness, basal sliding/flow intensity and direction, rock type/strength and fractures, pre-existing relief and substrate layers, subglacial water, erosional resistance, retained prior excavation and elapsed glacial exposure.
items.Fields & products written: Eroded rock and sediment packages in the shared Ground/material owner, changed bedrock and surface elevation, debris made available to glacier transport, and retained cumulative glacial erosion and scoured-bed evidence.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Ice movement supplies mechanical work; abrasion and plucking act through the common rock-material interaction contract, with basal water and rock resistance governing response. Removed mass enters the sediment/debris ledger; no decorative carving pass bypasses materials.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Historical periods with moving grounded ice, at World-scale and any finer map where actual local ice exposure is newly simulated. Refinement of an already glaciated landscape resolves inherited troughs and substrate without re-excavating the same completed interval.
items.Other process interactions: Ice-flow and mass balance set erosion opportunity; fracture/rock strata govern carving; deposition, meltwater, river incision, lakes, ocean inundation, later mass wasting and ecosystems modify the inherited glacial terrain.
items.Invariants / obligations: A stagnant or floating ice cover must not carve as a moving grounded glacier. Eroded volume has a material fate, existing crust and named landforms must remain causally continuous, and historical excavation must not be doubled on child refinement.
items.Review notes: Abrasion and plucking are distinct physical wear responses within one glacial-erosion phenomenon; landform naming/classification is downstream, not part of the excavation.

items.Semantic name: Glacial debris conveyance, release and moraine formation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Deposit glacially transported material on the land, building sediment cover and retaining deposition history.
items.Observable effects: Terminal and lateral moraines, hummocky till, erratic-rich forelands and sediment dams appear where ice slows, grounds, retreats or ends; glacial sediment helps divert streams, impound lakes and create later outwash plains.
items.Fields & products read: Glacially excavated rock/debris cargo and material composition, ice-flow paths and transport intensity, terminus/grounding and retreat history, substrate relief, sediment accommodation, water/sea outlets and inherited deposits.
items.Fields & products written: Transported glacial sediment and retained deposited Ground layers/packages, changed surface and sediment thickness, cumulative glacial deposition, moraine-forming topography and residual cargo handed to water or marine sediment pathways.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Receives material removed by glacial erosion; releases it through the shared material/transport ledger when ice loses capacity, with accommodation/terrain controlling deposition. Meltwater may sort and carry outwash under hydrologic sediment processes rather than conjuring new glacial cargo.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: During glacial advance, stagnation and retreat at any supported historical geological scope; present finer maps resolve the geometry and composition of inherited deposits, with external glacial cargo as a declared boundary input where needed.
items.Other process interactions: Erosion supplies cargo and ice flow transports it; meltwater, rivers and coasts rework deposited tills; moraines redirect drainage, form lakes and influence vegetation, soils, routes and settlements.
items.Invariants / obligations: No terminal moraine without a plausible debris source and flow/release history. Sediment is neither created by a landform classifier nor lost at a cropped boundary; distinguish unsorted ice-laid till from sorted meltwater deposits and avoid duplicating deposits at finer resolution.
items.Review notes: Owns movement and release of glacial debris within ice; waterborne outwash is coupled but remains a sediment-transport effect of meltwater.

items.Semantic name: Glacier and retained-snow meltwater release
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Contribute meltwater released by ice and retained snow to the water system.
items.Observable effects: Summer-fed streams, cold proglacial lakes, seasonal floods and melt-fed valleys reflect stored snow/ice and warming; strong melt pulses can rework till, carry sediment toward deltas and open passes formerly covered by ice.
items.Fields & products read: Retained snow and glacier ice storage, air/ground temperature and thaw, ice retreat and melt exposure, drainage directions and catchments, ice-covered surface continuity, parent/boundary inflow and water time step.
items.Fields & products written: Meltwater released to the water ledger and glacial runoff/inflow bands (including GlacialMeltwater), routed contributions to streams/lakes/coasts, and explicit calving, sublimation or boundary-transfer accounting as applicable.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Ice mass balance owns changes in long-lived ice reserves; the water system receives water released or annually supplied from snow on glaciers. Use a shared water-budget/transfer contract so rainfall, snowfall, ground storage and glacial melt cannot be counted twice.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Seasonal and climate-time hydrologic response over real connected catchments; finer maps can resolve local channels at the same final historical moment using inherited snow/ice and upstream meltwater discharge, not replay a completed epoch of deglaciation.
items.Other process interactions: Mass balance and ice motion define ice stores and pathways; runoff, lake basins, river channels, groundwater and sediment transport receive melt; outburst flooding and glacial retreat create later ecological and settlement consequences.
items.Invariants / obligations: Every water contribution must be accounted for as snow/ice melt, captured upstream inflow or documented external source. A cropped headwater cannot erase the glacier's melt contribution; distinguish recurring seasonal discharge from one-time geological retreat.
items.Review notes: A genuine water-transfer phenomenon with ice as the source; it does not own fresh glacier formation or the fluvial sediment mechanisms energized by that water.

items.Semantic name: Groundwater recharge, subsurface flow and baseflow return
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Infiltrate, retain, move, and return subsurface water, influencing water stores, recharge, and discharge to channels.
items.Observable effects: Rain sinks into permeable soils and fractured rock, sustains springs and perennial reaches after dry spells, raises or drains groundwater-fed wetlands and lake margins, and creates sharp contrasts where aquifers meet impermeable beds or magic-modified substrates.
items.Fields & products read: Precipitation and soil-water infiltration, retained groundwater and pore capacity, subsurface elevation/head, permeability of real rock and soil layers, fractures, vegetation use, water table, lakes and channel stage, inherited aquifer and outside-boundary recharge/discharge.
items.Fields & products written: Retained groundwater inventory, recharge and transfer volumes, flow targets and exchange paths, groundwater-to-river/lake/spring return and outflow fields; water-ledger records for transfers crossing domain or map boundaries.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Water's inventory/ledger owns quantities; substrate and magic supply material permeability as shared questions; runoff and rivers receive groundwater baseflow, and standing water can recharge aquifers. The geological and hydrological units must be interpreted consistently.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Historical or seasonal water-budget occurrence on a World; present head/flow solution and local recharge/return during bounded Region, City or Street refinement. Parent aquifer state and external head/flux are boundary conditions, not a fresh groundwater history.
items.Other process interactions: Runoff/soil infiltration feeds groundwater; rivers, wetlands, springs and lakes receive its return; fractures, tectonics, groundwater extraction, Hallowed protection and magic-altered stone redirect the flow. Eco/settlement viability responds to water persistence.
items.Invariants / obligations: Conserve water through recharge, storage, transfer, extraction and return, with explicit boundary terms; never produce baseflow from a dry disconnected cropped aquifer or reset inherited head to zero. No second rock-permeability or hydrological inventory owner.
items.Review notes: Independent subsurface hydrological mechanism. Distinguish effective groundwater storage/flow from a surface-water routing visualization; keep external connected aquifers represented by an initial/boundary provider.

items.Semantic name: Boundary-fed wave exposure for coastal erosion
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Supply and apply offshore wave/coastal attack arriving from outside the selected map footprint through the ordinary coastal abrasion and deposition phenomenon.
items.Observable effects: Sea-facing headlands, wave-cut fronts and vulnerable shorelines can continue responding to powerful remote storms or offshore Pressure even where a clipped map contains too little open ocean to generate that forcing internally; erosion and coastal debris remain physically situated.
items.Fields & products read: Captured or boundary-provided incident wave energy, direction, season/exposure and provenance; external offshore basin/current/Pressure context; actual source-connected shoreline, rock/material resistance and wave transmission geometry.
items.Fields & products written: Boundary wave-attack inputs and associated provenance, consumed by the shared coastal erosion/deposition process; when invoked with valid exposure, the ordinary material owner records beach/cliff wear, sediment movements and wave-attack legacy. No separate physical sediment inventory.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Explicit marine boundary provider feeds the same wave-energy/coastal-forcing questions as local fetch and current exposure. The shared coast/material operations apply abrasion and sediment deposition, so direct offshore and externally supplied force are not duplicated.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: A boundary-conditioned occurrence on exposed coast for World open edges and coastal Region/City/Street footprints. Current-state detail uses captured forcing without advancing another storm season or epoch; genuine elapsed coastal history must be scheduled explicitly.
items.Other process interactions: Pressure rays, offshore currents, winds, storm tracks and sea-level changes establish incoming energy; lithology and coastal vegetation govern resistance. Eroded material subsequently feeds littoral transport, marine settling and shoreline ecology.
items.Invariants / obligations: Never mistake the crop edge for a real coastline, invent waves from a nonexistent local ocean or apply the same offshore energy twice. External forcing must be traceable to an actual offshore source; abrasion and deposition obey the canonical material/shoreline rules.
items.Review notes: Boundary/coupling contract, not a second kind of erosion. It invokes the canonical coastal erosion phenomenon with offshore forcing supplied by the parent or adjacent ocean rather than duplicating physical logic.

items.Semantic name: Wave-driven shoreline erosion and littoral sediment redistribution
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Wear, remove, transport, and redeposit coastal material under wave exposure and shoreline conditions.
items.Observable effects: Exposed coasts retreat into headlands, cliffs and abrasion platforms while sheltered reaches accumulate beaches, bars and spits. Straits, coves, river mouths and natural harbors evolve in ways recognizable from rock resistance, wave direction and sediment supply.
items.Fields & products read: Active marine shoreline, sea stand and water depths; ocean waves, current/fetch exposure, storms and any explicit external offshore forcing; retained rock/sediment columns, hardness, fractures and slope; stabilizing cover, accumulated shore deposits and incoming/outgoing material cargo.
items.Fields & products written: Material-aware rock abrasion/plucking, coastal sediment pickup and littoral deposits, changed nearshore elevation and seabed substrate, coastline and exposure legacy, accumulated coastal erosion/deposition evidence, outgoing marine sediment loads and supported geomorphic features.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Wave-energy and coastal-forcing questions bind ocean currents, Pressure/magic and offshore boundary conditions; root-hold and rock-material modes determine resistance. All erosion and deposition use actual material transfer/receiving operations rather than an elevation-only paint effect.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World historical shoreline evolution with elapsed exposure. Region, coastal City or Street maps can resolve local beaches, coves and cliffs using inherited wave/material state and explicit cross-boundary delivery, not automatically another full historical duration.
items.Other process interactions: Ocean stand determines where waves attack; currents and storms set exposure, tectonic uplift and lithology set resistance, and fluvial deltas/marine sedimentation supply material. Altered coastal shape then affects wetlands, sea access, settlement sites and maritime networks.
items.Invariants / obligations: Coastal sediment must originate in rock, mobile cover, river cargo or marine load; deposits have a supported receiving shore and provenance. Differentiate exposed from sheltered coasts and avoid adding geomorphic age on successive refinements. Keep established named coasts and landforms recognizable while resolving their shape.
items.Review notes: One physical phenomenon with multiple strategies and exposure providers. External-coastal-forcing is the boundary-driven occurrence of this same process; deep-seabed gravity settling and river delta formation have separate causal owners.

items.Semantic name: Glacial landform interpretation from retained physical evidence
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Realize identifiable glacial landforms from the terrain and retained evidence created by ice flow, erosion and deposition.
items.Observable effects: Maps distinguish cirques, glacial troughs and U-shaped valleys, moraine belts, overdeepened basins and other ice-shaped places where inherited erosion, transported debris and valley geometry support them; named glacial features can persist through finer mapping.
items.Fields & products read: Recorded maximum ice extent and thickness, grounded ice-flow history, cumulative glacial abrasion and deposition, rock and terrain morphology, river and lake context, parent glacial feature identity and relevant mapping scale.
items.Fields & products written: Interpreted glacial landform classes and evidence-linked feature candidates/anchors; stable named GIS landforms are emitted by the separate geographic publication owner. No new ice, sediment or excavated rock is created.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Reads evidence supplied by ice flow, erosion, sediment deposition and drainage. Its classifier evaluates characteristic geometry and history; it does not feed back extra glacier motion or generate missing material to justify a label.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Present-state interpretation at World/Region/City/Street where resolution supports recognizable forms; finer realization clarifies inherited shapes and feature footprints without repeating a glaciation epoch.
items.Other process interactions: Receives actual glacial sculpture and deposits; intersects river valleys, postglacial lakes, marine inundation, generic landform classification and durable landmark/GIS identity.
items.Invariants / obligations: A glacial label needs relevant history and compatible morphology, not just elevation or arbitrary noise. Do not overwrite the underlying material state or replace a recognized named feature simply because finer cells classify differently; interpret rather than cause glaciation.
items.Review notes: Classification/geographic realization contract, not an ice-scouring process or independent GIS publisher. Preserve evidence and named-feature continuity across resolution changes.

items.Semantic name: Marine sea-ice formation, persistence and seasonal breakup
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Determine sea-ice presence or suitability from marine water and temperature conditions.
items.Observable effects: Winter pack ice, recurring ice-edge zones and persistent polar cover affect exposed coasts, marine travel, waves, freezing harbors and marine habitats; warming, currents and wave attack create open leads and retreating margins.
items.Fields & products read: Connected marine water/sea stand, seasonal air and sea temperature, ocean heat, currents and wave exposure, prior sea-ice thickness/persistence, external pack-ice edge conditions and thermal/magic inputs.
items.Fields & products written: Sea-ice thickness and cover/suitability, recurring or persistent sea-ice extent and ice-margin context; exchanged frozen/freshwater and heat obligations where material ocean/ice storage changes.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Ocean circulation, sea-surface warmth and wave conditions govern freezing and breakup; Aurora persistence or Fire warmth changes the applicable physical rule through shared questions. Sea ice attenuates waves and changes ecological and navigational access without becoming a grounded valley glacier.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Ocean seasonal and climate-epoch change wherever connected sea is present, with finer coastal refinement resolving inherited ice extent and externally continued pack ice. No fresh centuries-long freeze pass solely because a child is drawn.
items.Other process interactions: Ocean currents and atmospheric climate drive ice; ice feeds coastal wave exposure, ocean heat, water budgets, habitat and settlement access. Shoreline freezing is distinct from land-ice erosion, calving and glacier-derived river meltwater.
items.Invariants / obligations: Form ice only over a valid marine surface with appropriate heat exchange; persistent ice needs climatic or inherited support. Preserve sea-ice continuity at cropped ocean boundaries, keep frozen-water accounting coherent, and never ascribe glacial bedrock excavation to floating pack ice.
items.Review notes: Treat a physically retained sea-ice cover as the semantic phenomenon; suitability and visual ice flags are supporting observations, not substitutes for changing marine ice state.

items.Semantic name: Landform interpretation from retained relief and history
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Classify landform character from terrain, water bodies, drainage, slope, and geomorphic evidence.
items.Observable effects: A player can distinguish ridges and named peaks, scarps, plateaus, mountain shoulders, river-cut valleys, glacial troughs, basins, headlands and other recognizable forms where their shapes and histories support them. A prominent summit remains identifiable above its surrounding ridge.
items.Fields & products read: Present elevation, rock/relief and slope, water and mapped rivers, geomorphic histories (uplift, fluvial/glacial/coastal incision, deposition, impacts), prominence and neighboring relief, existing named landform identities and spatial context extending beyond crop edges.
items.Fields & products written: Derived landform codes, candidate extents, prominence/evidence and relationship hints for geographic publication. No new rock, relief, ice, water or historical event is created by this classifier.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Reads the shared physical and geomorphic evidence produced by actual processes and passes qualified shapes to geographic significance and named-feature/GIS owners. More local scale reveals finer morphology without treating a classification algorithm as a geomorphic force.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Present-state interpretation for World, Region, City and Street when geographic evidence/resolution supports the feature; a child refines extents and subfeatures from captured parent relief/history instead of generating a new physical past.
items.Other process interactions: Tectonic construction, erosion, glacial sculpture, river networks, coastal changes and material stratigraphy create forms; placement of landmarks/POIs and travel/culture can use their recognized locations and significance.
items.Invariants / obligations: Every label must be compatible with real current terrain and retained causal evidence; no self-fulfilling sculpting to meet a label. Named peaks or valleys do not disappear at finer scales just because a coarse recognition threshold fails; preserve stable identities.
items.Review notes: Classification / derived geography, not GIS publication or an alternative mechanism for making mountains and valleys. Feature extraction should not silently mutate Ground.

items.Semantic name: River channel form and hydraulic capacity
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Resolve the physical width, depth, strength, and thermal character of channels from the river network and flow.
items.Observable effects: Rivers of equal mapped order develop different widths, depths, channel banks, pools, riffles and thermal reach behavior according to actual discharge, bank materials and gradient. Physical crossings and settlements respond to the reachable depth and flow, not a decorative line.
items.Fields & products read: Retained river reach identities and paths, seasonal discharge and flood persistence, valley gradient and bed elevation, rock/soil bank resistance, sediment supply and deposition, water temperature/geothermal inputs, inherited channel dimensions and upstream/downstream reach context.
items.Fields & products written: Hydraulic channel width/depth, channel strength or conveyance, bank-contact and reach geometry, locally conditioned channel warmth; significant channel-form features ready for real-scale realization. Does not independently excavate historical rock mass.
items.Shared questions / coupling: River-network/catchment owner supplies actual reaches and water volumes; Ground/material questions supply bank strength and incision susceptibility. A geometry strategy may invoke material-backed channel adjustment only through fluvial erosion/deposition contracts.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: World and Region hydraulic reach characteristics, with more accurate City/Street footprints at real dimensions. Recompute present hydraulics at finer resolution from inherited connected rivers and supplied discharge, not new centuries of widening.
items.Other process interactions: Runoff, groundwater, lakes, floodplains and delta outlets condition discharge; fluvial incision and sediment transport change the actual bed/banks; real-scale pools, ford depths, bridges, fishing and waterborne travel consume channel geometry.
items.Invariants / obligations: Width, depth and conveyance must be compatible with flow, real units, bed material and inherited reach identity. No zero-width river because a local crop lacks upstream catchment; geometry must not duplicate sediment removal counted by erosion.
items.Review notes: Hydraulic/geographic mechanism with distinct material effects only via the rock/sediment owners; preserve the distinction between real channel dimensions and the GIS stroke width of a published river.

items.Semantic name: Floodplain exposure and overbank-zone interpretation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Identify land exposed to river flooding and characterize floodplain extent or intensity around channels.
items.Observable effects: Low adjoining valley floors, meander belts, natural levees and flats are recognized as flood-exposed to varying degree; farmland, wetlands, villages and roads experience consistent recurring inundation risk and alluvial opportunities.
items.Fields & products read: Established river network and flood-season discharge, water levels and overbank channel capacity, valley-floor relief and slope, catchment membership, sedimentary/alluvial history, vegetation/obstructions, parent floodplain extents and upstream flood-wave context.
items.Fields & products written: Derived floodplain reach/intensity bands, overbank influence areas and hazard/opportunity context for ecology, land occupation and location significance. Actual water and sediment changes remain with water transfer and material-deposition processes.
items.Shared questions / coupling: River hydraulics determines whether/where overflow reaches adjacent terrain; shared flood/inundation questions expose the resulting risk and opportunities to ecology, soil, settlements and landmark/crossing siting. Do not equate the indicator itself with a flood event.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Present/seasonal floodplain evaluation at World, Region, City and Street scales as geographic fidelity permits; child floodplains retain parent valley and upstream flood context without redoing historic floods or turning clipped tributaries into dry gullies.
items.Other process interactions: Runoff peaks, river-channel form, lake releases, ice melt and levees govern exposure. Fluvial deposition and erosion gradually create the floodplain materials; ecology and human land use interpret fertile, wet or dangerous zones.
items.Invariants / obligations: Floodplain location must follow real hydraulic connectivity and available relief, not proximity to any river line alone. Do not award alluvial soil, build levees or remove sediment just by publishing a floodplain label; named feature extents may be refined, not erased.
items.Review notes: Derived flood-risk and terrain-interpretation contract, not a second floodwater or depositional process. A genuinely simulated flood episode would have its own water/material transfer through the existing owners.

items.Semantic name: River-delta morphology and mouth-deposition interpretation
items.Responsibility / phenomenon: Identify and characterize deltas where river networks discharge into standing marine water.
items.Observable effects: Where sustained rivers deliver sediment faster than marine waves and currents remove it, marshes, bars, distributary fans and shallow delta-front deposits become identifiable; low-sediment or strongly swept mouths remain estuaries or open coasts.
items.Fields & products read: Identified river mouths and coastal water connections, actual river-borne sediment cargo and deposition history, discharge and flood pulse, delta-front relief/shelf depth, ocean currents/wave reworking, subsidence and relative sea level, inherited named delta identity.
items.Fields & products written: Recognized delta footprint/intensity and morphology candidates with links to their river and sedimentary origin; GIS publication may delineate a named delta. No independent source of rock/sediment or duplicate mouth-bed deposition.
items.Shared questions / coupling: Sediment-transport and marine/coastal deposition owners form the actual deltaic land via their material ledger. This interpretation reads their resulting shallow ground and supply; a dedicated future delta-progradation process must reuse that material rather than adding a second delta budget.
items.Spatial & temporal scope: Long-time geological delta recognition and present World/Region/City/Street refinement. Capture parent delta/river-mouth identity and offshore sediment/bathymetry context; refinement sharpens branches and bars without recreating accumulated alluvium.
items.Other process interactions: River-network evolution and sediment transport supply distributaries and deposition, while tides/currents/waves redistribute loads. Delta wetlands and coast shape ecology, harbors, settlement risk and crossings.
